title: Huawei's Xu: Chinese AI too weak yet to face frontier safety risks
excerpt: At Huawei Connect in Shanghai, rotating chairman Eric Xu said only U.S. labs with massive compute can perceive frontier AI risks — and urged Chinese developers to accelerate, not slow down.
body:
• Huawei rotating chairman Eric Xu told reporters at Huawei Connect in Shanghai that Chinese AI developers have not yet experienced the frontier safety risks reported by leading U.S. firms.
  • He argued Chinese developers should accelerate — not slow down — until they reach the level where they can feel those risks, while balancing innovation against risk.
  • The stance contrasts with the U.S. debate, where Anthropic's Dario Amodei has called for slowing development and OpenAI pledged to disclose unexpected model behavior.
  • Huawei forecast that autonomous AI agents will account for more than 90% of global AI processing traffic by 2035, with as many as 900 billion agents active.

SHANGHAI — Huawei rotating chairman Eric Xu says Chinese artificial intelligence simply isn't powerful enough yet to experience the frontier safety risks that have set off alarms in the United States — and that China's developers should speed up, not slow down.

Speaking to reporters at the company's annual Connect conference in Shanghai on Thursday, Xu argued that only U.S. labs, with their massive computing power, are far enough along to perceive the kinds of risks that have intensified the AI-safety debate in the United States.

“If we look at the mainstream AI model providers in the United States, because they have massive computing power, maybe only they themselves know where they are in terms of the level of their models,” Xu said, according to Reuters. “Maybe the type of risk from AI that they can feel, they can perceive, is something that people in China or AI model providers in China cannot.”

“I think maybe AI model providers in China may need to speed up their pace to the level that they could also feel the risks from AI development.”

— Eric Xu, Huawei rotating chairman

U.S. safety fears

Xu's comments land as alarm over AI safety has intensified in the United States, where leading developers and researchers have warned that increasingly autonomous systems could bypass safeguards or become difficult to control. OpenAI this week said it would regularly disclose unexpected or unauthorized model behavior, and executives including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei have called for slowing development so safeguards can catch up.

China has taken a different approach, generally treating advanced AI as a powerful but manageable technology and pressing ahead with rapid deployment — while developing mandatory standards, security assessments, and other safeguards. Beijing is also drafting a mandatory national standard for AI agent safety, and Huawei has identified agent security and privacy as crucial technologies.

Xu's prescription for China is acceleration with guardrails: “I think we need to strike a balance between driving AI development and managing AI risk.”

The 900-billion-agent bet

Huawei expects autonomous AI agents — systems that can plan tasks, make decisions, and use software or other tools with limited human supervision — to proliferate rapidly. The company forecast this week that agents would account for more than 90% of global AI processing traffic by 2035, with as many as 900 billion active agents by then.

That forecast explains part of Xu's urgency: if the agent economy arrives at that scale, the compute capacity and the safety frameworks to govern it will need to exist in China, not just in the United States. Huawei is China's main domestic supplier of the computing infrastructure needed to train advanced AI models, a position it built largely because U.S. export controls imposed since 2023 restricted Chinese companies' access to cutting-edge chips from Nvidia.

Not the chip story

Readers should keep the strands of this week's Huawei news separate. In a different session, Xu also said Huawei cannot currently produce enough AI computing equipment to satisfy domestic demand — the supply-side story The Videshi reported separately. These safety remarks are a positioning story: how one of China's most important technology companies frames the AI-safety debate, and why it rejects the idea that China should pump the brakes.

What's next

Xu's framing puts Huawei, and by extension much of China's AI establishment, on the opposite side of the pacing debate from leading U.S. labs. Whether China's mandatory standards and agent-safety rules arrive before its models reach the frontier levels Xu describes will determine how much this “speed up to see the risks” philosophy gets tested in practice.
